name: Combined oral contraceptive pill for acne

card.summary: Estrogen-plus-progestin birth control pills that the FDA has cleared for moderate acne in women who also want contraception; effective for many, with clotting risk attached.
card.aka: The pill for acne; COC; Yaz, Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz
card.note: Prescription-only; raises venous clotting risk, with differences by progestin.

quick.overview:
Combined oral contraceptive pills contain an estrogen and a progestin. Because they lower androgen activity, some formulations are used to treat acne in women, and the US FDA has approved four of them for moderate acne in patients who also need contraception.

It is a hormonal option discussed in dermatology rather than a looksmaxxing-specific protocol, and is relevant only to people who can use these pills.
quick.mechanism: The estrogen component suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone-binding globulin, which lowers free testosterone. Lower androgens reduce sebum production, a driver of acne [1].
quick.risks: Common effects include breakthrough bleeding, nausea, headache and breast tenderness. Venous thromboembolism risk is raised in users and varies by progestin, and arterial events are increased in smokers over 35 and people with migraine with aura. The FDA added a label warning for drospirenone-containing pills in 2012 [1].

lead: Combined oral contraceptive pills combine an estrogen with a progestin and are taken mainly to prevent pregnancy. Dermatologists also prescribe them for acne in women, because the hormonal changes they cause lower sebum production and, with it, breakouts. For people who can use them, the appearance payoff is clearer, less oily skin and fewer inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions on the face.[1]

Wikipedia reports that studies show combined pills reduce both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions, that head-to-head comparisons between brands have not been studied, and that progestin-only pills have not been shown to help acne.[1] Its acne article cites reductions in lesions of 40 to 70 percent in studies, and a 2014 review in which oral antibiotics were somewhat more effective than the pills for inflammatory lesions at three months, with the two roughly equal by six months.[2]

The US FDA has approved four combined pills for moderate acne in patients aged at least 14 or 15 who have started menstruating and need contraception: Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz and YAZ.[1] A 2012 Lancet review of acne treatment described combined pills as able to help women with acne, with isotretinoin named as the most effective option overall.[4]

chain: Fewer acne lesions and less oily skin
angle.text: For women with hormonally driven acne, such as flares around periods, adult-onset acne or oily skin, the pill reduces androgen effects on the oil glands and can clear the face over several months. It is used on its own or alongside topical treatments.

paras: The FDA-approved acne indication applies to moderate acne in patients who have started menstruating and who also seek oral contraception.[1] Hormonal treatments including combined pills are described in Wikipedia's acne article as options that may be considered first-line when a woman wants contraception, shows signs of excess androgens, has adult-onset acne, premenstrual flares, or significant oiliness.[2] Apart from acne, the FDA has approved no oral contraceptives for other conditions the pill is commonly used to treat.[1]

The acne article reports that third- and fourth-generation progestins such as desogestrel, dienogest, drospirenone and norgestimate, and pills containing cyproterone acetate or chlormadinone acetate, have stronger antiandrogenic effects, while first-generation progestins such as norethindrone and norgestrel may worsen acne.[2]

A 2012 Lancet review noted that good-quality comparative evidence for acne treatments is scarce, while stating that combined pills can help women with acne.[4] The 2014 comparison with oral antibiotics found antibiotics somewhat ahead on inflammatory lesions at three months, with roughly equal results at six months; the review's authors suggested pills may suit some women as a first-line option because they do not drive antibiotic resistance.[2]
The most common side effect is breakthrough bleeding, followed by nausea, headache, bloating, breast tenderness and weight or fluid changes, which often fade with time.[1]

Wikipedia reports venous thromboembolism risk of roughly 60 per 100,000 woman-years in users versus 30 in non-users, varying by progestin, with higher rate ratios than levonorgestrel for desogestrel, gestodene, drospirenone and cyproterone acetate.[1] An FDA review of drospirenone pills led to a 2012 label warning.[1] Ischemic stroke and heart attack risk is increased, especially with high estrogen doses, smoking over 35 or migraine with aura.[1] Contraindications include pregnancy, hypertension, prior thrombosis and liver tumours.[1]

Progestogen feedback reduces GnRH pulses, lowering FSH and LH and preventing ovulation. For acne, estrogen lowers ovarian androgen production, raises SHBG and decreases free testosterone, and sebaceous glands shrink.[1][2]
Oral contraceptives were first approved by the FDA for contraception in 1960. Later generations lowered estrogen dose and varied the progestin.[1]

Wikipedia summarises studies as showing reduced inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial lesions with combined pills, but notes no direct brand comparisons.[1] A 2014 review compared pills with oral antibiotics for acne lesion counts at three and six months.[2] The 2012 Lancet acne review concluded that combined pills can help women with acne.[4] A registered post-authorisation study of YAZ in China enrolled 1,921 participants, with contraception rather than acne as the studied condition.[3]

timeline.event: First oral contraceptive approved by the FDA.[1]
FDA adds a label warning on VTE risk for drospirenone-containing pills.[1]
